questions.knowledge_point: Finding Particular Solutions of Differential Equations by First Rearranging and Then Separating
questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x-2y}$ that satisfies $y(0)=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{x-2y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{-2y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2y}} \\ {e}^{2y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{x} \\ \int {e}^{2y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2y} & ={e}^{x}+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{2y} & =2{e}^{x}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2{C}_{1}$ is an arbitrary constant.

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{e}^{x}+C) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{e}^{x}+C).\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(0)=0$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{e}^{0}+C) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2+C) & =0 \\ 2+C & =1 \\ C & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x-2y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=0$ is

$$
y=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{e}^{x}-1).
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2yx+y{x}^{2}$ that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2yx+y{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(2x+{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x+{x}^{2} \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =2\int x\,\text{d}x+\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & ={x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ y & =\pm {e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ y & =K{e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=1$ to find $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =1 \\ K{e}^{{1}^{2}+{1}^{3}/3} & =1 \\ K{e}^{4/3} & =1 \\ K & ={e}^{-4/3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2yx+y{x}^{2}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y={e}^{-4/3}\cdot {e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3}={e}^{({x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-4)/3}\,.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{x}$ that satisfies $y(1)=2.$ Assume that $x>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{x} \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x} \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ \frac{1}{y} & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Assuming $x>0,$ the general solution is

$$
y=-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+C},
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now apply the condition $y(1)=2$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =2 \\ -\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡1+C} & =2 \\ -\frac{1}{C} & =2 \\ C & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{x}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=2$ is

$$
y=\frac{-1}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{1}{2})}=\frac{2}{1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\,.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}$  that satisfies $y(1)=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} \\ {y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2} \\ \int {y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{2}\,\text{d}y & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{y}^{3}}{3} & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{C}_{1} \\ {y}^{3} & ={x}^{3}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where   $C=3{C}_{1}$ is an arbitrary constant.  

We now apply the condition $y(1)=2$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{3} & ={1}^{3}+C \\ 8-1 & =C \\ C & =7\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
{y}^{3}={x}^{3}+7.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $(\frac{1}{xy}-\frac{1}{x})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2$ that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{1}{xy}-\frac{1}{x})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2 \\ \frac{1}{x}(\frac{1}{y}-1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2 \\ (\frac{1}{y}-1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ \int (\frac{1}{y}-1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y|-y & ={x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|1|-1 & ={1}^{2}+C \\ 0-1 & =1+C \\ C & =-2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $(\frac{1}{xy}-\frac{1}{x})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ in implicit form is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|-y={x}^{2}-2\,.
$$
